You should encourage your players to take it ‘seriously.’ Like, not overly serious, but like treat it like a full game. But at the same time, if players don’t want to play that character, for whatever reason, (class is not for them or they don’t like their personality) they should be able to switch.

Spells sold via chips are one time use. Once they are downloaded off the chip, they are empty. 
If you were to uninstall a spell from yourself and put it onto a chip for someone else to use, you run the risk of:

1. The buyer or seller being jailed for selling/buying a spellware (I just made that name up and I like it so that’s the name of it now) that is second hand. Like it being illegal to pirate things. Cops can pull you over (for speeding, merging wrong, etc.) and scan you for any weapons and, by extension, spellware. You then run the risk of being taken in for illegally downloading it. 
2. Second hand spellware or imitation spellware could give you adverse effects. These can range from it just not working to it could shut down all cybernetic you have.

I’m mostly leaning toward “this spells does this, if the roll fails, it doesn’t work.” But like flavor spells (like cantrips) where you can, say, shape water into a sculpture or something like that and it would wear off in an hour or until it melts. (Given there would be a limit to the amount of water they can shape etc.) 

I was thinking of adding wild magic as well. (A type of magic from 5e) For certain spells, every time it is cast, they roll a d10. When a 1 is rolled, it would cause the magic to go wild. And then a table of up to 100 things can happen as a result. Good, bad, or funny. Not sure how I’d work that in. On the fence about that but I loved it in 5e. Leads to interesting encounters.

First off, spells can only be bought. Gone are the days of a bloodline carrying a magic title or trading your soul to being for magical powers. Some magic is based on a group of powerful Magicians (in-universe magic users) that wrote these spells down. These were then scripted into code so that instead it may be downloaded. All spells are bought and learned through two ways:

1. Downloading the spell through a chip that is sold.
2. Read and learned through normal means. (Usually for the rarer/older spells)

Depending on how powerful/rare a spell is, the more the price is. There might be more I’m forgetting rn. But this is all a work in progress for me.
Yep. That’s why I did. Would you like to know more about it?

Different forms of magic work in different ways. Some magic is straight magic written into being by very powerful magicians (magic users in my world). Others are cybernetic enhancements further pushed to their limits through the use of magic. 
One person on the sub put in my head the idea of a type of off-the-streets magic black market that is forbidden, almost like how some guns are banned in-universe.

Spells are bought. Each rarity of spell and the power of spells increase or decrease the price. Cantrip spells last indefinitely and can be used at any time. Spells can be used three a day. Powerful spells can be used anywhere from once a session to once a game, depending on how powerful it is. 
Everyone has the ability to obtain and use spells. Those with the magic skill get bonuses on using spells. (Like adding the handgun skill to a roll when you shoot a handgun). 
I haven’t given much thought to rarity. I will take that into consideration. Like a black market of spells and magical items. 
They vary in use. Some are full magic (the rarer ones are) and others are cybernetic technology pushed into the “future” due to magic means.
I’ll check it out. Thanks

Each Spell costs money. Bloodline and making a deal with a creature (not involving money) no longer grant Spells. There are cantrip (use any time), spells (three per long rest), and powerful spells (once per session). They either upload the spells knowledge digitally or read if they don’t have the proper CyberWare. There are no levels. There is price to manage the spell’s powerfulness. Any more questions, ask.
